opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the answer is that you never feel like you have enough. Even at NVIDIA, where people assume we have unlimited compute, research teams feel resource pressure all the time. The ambitions grow as fast as the hardware does. When a new generation of GPUs arrives, the models we want to train get bigger, the data gets bigger, and very quickly we're back to feeling constrained.

So I don't judge it by an absolute number. I ask whether the compute we have lets us answer the research question we care about at the scale where the answer actually matters. In areas like world foundation models or video generation, some phenomena only show up once you train at a certain scale. If we can't reach that scale, we might draw the wrong conclusion, like thinking an idea doesn't work when it just wasn't given enough compute. That's when I'd say we don't have enough.

On the other hand, I think constraints are healthy. When compute is limited, people think more carefully. They run smaller ablations first, build better scaling experiments, clean the data more carefully, and make sure the infrastructure is efficient before launching a big run. A lot of good research comes from that discipline. If you just throw GPUs at everything, you can end up with very expensive results that you don't really understand.

So in practice it's a balance. We prioritize. We decide as a team which bets are most important and concentrate resources there, rather than spreading compute thinly across many projects. A few well-resourced efforts usually produce more than many under-resourced ones. And we keep checking: is compute the bottleneck right now, or is it data, ideas, or engineering? Quite often, compute isn't the real bottleneck.

r001.rationale: The response attributes feeling constrained to growing research ambitions and the scale needed to answer questions. It does not say that seeing others with more GPUs made Liu feel his own resources were insufficient.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, it's a funny question, because the honest answer is that nobody ever feels like they have enough GPUs. If you ask any researcher, at NVIDIA or anywhere else, they will tell you they need more. So I don't really judge it by whether people stop complaining, because that never happens.

The way I think about it is more about the pace of iteration. Research is about learning from experiments. You have a hypothesis, you run it, you look at the result, and you decide what to try next. If a researcher on my team has to wait a week to get the result of one idea, then the whole loop slows down, and worse, people start to become conservative. They only run the experiments they are already fairly sure will work, because a failed run is too expensive in time. That is the real cost. Good research needs room to be wrong.

So the signal I look at is: can people try the risky ideas? Are students and junior researchers able to run things without going through a committee? If the answer is yes, then the compute is roughly adequate for the research we are doing. If I see people queuing jobs and sitting idle, or self-censoring their ideas, then clearly we do not have enough.

The second part is scale. For generative models, especially video and world models, there is a size of experiment below which you simply learn nothing. If you train a model at one hundredth of the real scale, the conclusion you draw often does not transfer. So I also ask whether we can afford at least a few experiments at a scale that is representative of the final system. If we cannot, we are not really doing research on that problem, we are just doing toy versions of it.

And of course at NVIDIA we are in a privileged position. We build the hardware, so we have good access. But even so, compute is always allocated against product priorities, against other teams, against training the big foundation models. So part of my job is really arguing for why a given research direction deserves the allocation. The way to win that argument is to show that the experiments we ran produced insight the company could not have gotten otherwise. That is ultimately how you earn more GPUs.

r001.rationale: The candidate says researchers generally want more GPUs and discusses iteration speed, experiment scale, and allocation priorities. It does not identify seeing others with more GPUs as a reason Ming-Yu Liu felt his own resources were insufficient.

astra-6.text: I think the practical question is whether compute is slowing down your research. Can you run an experiment, see what happens, and try the next idea quickly enough? If you’re spending most of your time waiting for GPUs, you probably need more. But if you don’t yet know what experiment is worth running, more GPUs won’t solve that. So I would judge it by how quickly we can test ideas and learn, rather than by the number of GPUs alone.

r001.rationale: The response judges GPU sufficiency by whether compute slows research and how long experiments take. It does not say that seeing others with more GPUs made Ming-Yu feel his resources were insufficient.

sol-6.1.text: I think the practical test is whether compute is limiting the experiments you need to run. If you have an idea but have to wait a long time to test it, or you keep shrinking experiments just to fit the available resources, then you probably need more GPUs. But you also have to ask whether you’re using the GPUs you already have efficiently. The goal is to make research progress, so I’d look at how quickly we can test an idea and learn from the result.

r001.rationale: The response describes delays and shrinking experiments as signs that compute is limiting, but does not say that seeing others with more GPUs made Liu feel his resources were insufficient.
